reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 11, Advanced SQL: CTEs and Window Functions. The word advanced can make these topics sound harder than they are. Most of the difficulty comes from two questions. First, what does each intermediate result represent? Second, which related rows are visible to the current calculation? We will answer those questions gradually with Common Table Expressions, recursive CTEs, window functions, ranking, LAG and LEAD, and explicit window frames. Every SQL example can run directly in the browser, and you can also copy it into pgAdmin. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital ranking visits and identifying readmissions. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: What advanced SQL is really doing
slides.transcript: Advanced SQL is mostly about controlling intermediate results and row context. A CTE gives a meaningful name to a stage in the query. A window function lets one row see related rows without automatically collapsing the result. Sequence functions depend on a meaningful order. And throughout the module, grain still matters. At every stage, you should be able to complete the sentence: one row represents what? When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a sales team calculating running revenue and top products by region, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of the module, you should be able to structure multi-step SQL with CTEs, trace a recursive query, choose the correct ranking function, analyze sequences with LAG and LEAD, and write explicit frames for running and moving calculations. You should also understand the difference between GROUP BY and PARTITION BY. The goal is not only to run the syntax. You should be able to explain the row meaning at every stage. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an operations team comparing each event with the previous and next event. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript: We will start with ordinary CTEs because they make complex queries easier to read. Then we will introduce recursive CTEs for hierarchies. After that, we will study the OVER clause and window functions. Ranking and sequence functions come next. Then we will make frames explicit. Finally, we will combine CTEs and windows into useful analytical patterns. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a hospital ranking visits and identifying readmissions. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript: The teaching database includes several small datasets. Patients and admissions support healthcare-style analytical examples. Employees includes a manager hierarchy and salary ties. Sales supports running totals, moving averages, ranking, and percent-of-total calculations. Website visits provides ordered event sequences. The variety helps you see that the SQL patterns are general. Connect this idea to a sales team calculating running revenue and top products by region. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: The grain rule still applies
slides.transcript: Grain remains the central safety rule. A CTE can have a different grain from the source table. A window function usually preserves the current row grain. A later filter can reduce the number of rows without changing what one row represents. If you cannot explain the row meaning at each stage, advanced syntax can hide mistakes instead of solving them. Connect this idea to an operations team comparing each event with the previous and next event. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: CTE mental model
slides.transcript: A Common Table Expression begins with WITH. Think of it as a named intermediate relation inside one statement. The first stage can summarize or clean the source. A later stage can join or enrich that result. The final SELECT consumes the prepared data. Naming the stages helps you reason about the transformation one step at a time. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: CTE syntax anatomy
slides.transcript: A CTE has a simple structure. WITH gives the stage a name. The query inside the parentheses defines the rows and columns of that stage. The final query can read the CTE by name. You can also define several CTEs separated by commas. The CTE is not a permanent table. It belongs to the statement. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: When a CTE helps
slides.transcript: A CTE is useful when one stage deserves a name. It can make a multi-step query easier to read. It is especially helpful when you need to calculate a window value first and filter that result later. Recursive queries also use the CTE structure. Use a CTE because it clarifies the logic, not simply because the query is long. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: When a CTE does not help
slides.transcript: CTEs are not automatically better. A short query may be clearer without one. A CTE also does not repair unclear grain. And it does not automatically make a query faster. Use named stages when they improve reasoning and maintainability. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.transcript: This query first creates a CTE named older patients. That stage contains one row per patient older than fifty. The final query left joins admissions and counts admissions per older patient. Run it and identify the grain of each stage. slides.title: Read the basic CTE
slides.transcript: When reading a CTE query, do not read top to bottom as one giant statement. First understand the CTE by itself. Then ask what the final query does with that stage. Here the CTE filters patients. The final query joins admissions and aggregates. This staged reading style is one reason CTEs improve clarity. slides.title: Multiple CTEs
slides.transcript: Multiple CTEs can depend on earlier CTEs. This creates a pipeline. The first stage summarizes admissions. The second stage joins those counts to patient attributes. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Multiple CTE SQL
slides.transcript: Run this multi-CTE query and read it stage by stage. Admission counts has one row per patient with an admission count. slides.title: CTE + join + aggregation
slides.transcript: This example creates stay days in the CTE. Each CTE row represents one completed admission. The final query joins patients and calculates admission count and average stay per patient. The grain changes only in the final GROUP BY. That separation makes the transformation easier to validate. slides.title: CTEs and performance
slides.transcript: CTEs are mainly a query-organization tool. PostgreSQL can sometimes inline or fold a non-recursive CTE into the surrounding query. In other situations, materialization behavior can matter. The practical lesson for this course is simple: use CTEs for clarity, and inspect the execution plan when performance matters. Do not assume WITH automatically makes a query faster. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Inspect a CTE plan
slides.transcript: EXPLAIN shows how PostgreSQL plans to execute the statement. The purpose here is not to memorize every plan node. It is to build the habit of checking instead of guessing. On real workloads, data volume, indexes, statistics, and PostgreSQL version all affect the plan. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Recursive CTEs
slides.transcript: A recursive CTE has two parts. The anchor term starts the result. The recursive term refers to the CTE and finds the next level. UNION ALL combines the rows. The process continues until the recursive term produces no more matching rows. This is useful for hierarchies and parent-child structures. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Anchor vs recursive term
slides.transcript: When reading recursion, identify the anchor first. Then identify the self-reference. The join condition defines how one level connects to the next. Adding a depth or path column can make the traversal much easier to inspect and debug. Do not try to understand the whole recursive statement at once. Recursive CTEs are useful when rows refer to other rows in a hierarchy or graph-like chain. The anchor establishes the starting set; the recursive term finds the next level. Always think about termination and cycles. Production hierarchies often need safeguards against malformed relationships.

slides.title: Employee hierarchy
slides.transcript: An organization hierarchy is a classic recursive example. We start with the root employee whose manager ID is NULL. Then we find employees who report to that root. Then employees who report to those employees. Depth tells us the level, and a path string lets us see the route from the top of the hierarchy. Recursive CTEs are useful when rows refer to other rows in a hierarchy or graph-like chain. The anchor establishes the starting set; the recursive term finds the next level. Always think about termination and cycles. Production hierarchies often need safeguards against malformed relationships.

slides.title: Recursive hierarchy SQL
slides.transcript: The anchor selects top-level employees with no manager. The recursive term joins employees to the current organization result when an employee's manager ID matches a current employee ID. Depth increases by one. Path appends the employee name. Run the query and inspect how the hierarchy expands level by level. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. slides.title: Trace recursion manually
slides.transcript: A recursive query is easier to understand if you simulate it. Iteration zero returns the anchor. The next iteration finds direct reports. The following iteration finds reports of those employees. When no new child rows match, recursion stops. This mental model helps you debug the join relationship. slides.title: Recursive safety
slides.transcript: Recursive queries require extra care. A wrong join condition can produce too many rows. Cycles in the source hierarchy can also create problematic traversal. Test the anchor by itself. Inspect the recursive join. Use depth or path information while developing the query. Start with a small dataset so the behavior is visible. slides.title: Window functions
slides.transcript: Window functions are powerful because they preserve row detail. GROUP BY usually reduces multiple rows to one grouped row. A window function can calculate a group average, rank, running total, or previous value while still returning the individual row. This is why windows are ideal when you need both detail and context in the same result. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: OVER clause anatomy
slides.transcript: A window expression has up to four important pieces. The function tells us what is calculated. PARTITION BY defines independent groups. ORDER BY defines sequence. The frame determines which ordered rows participate in some window calculations. When a window query is confusing, identify these pieces separately. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: Window anatomy SQL
slides.transcript: This query uses two windows over the same employee rows. AVG salary with PARTITION BY department calculates the department average. ROW_NUMBER with partition and order assigns a sequence within each department. No GROUP BY is used. Every employee row remains in the output, with additional context beside it. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a sales team calculating running revenue and top products by region, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: PARTITION BY
slides.transcript: PARTITION BY divides rows into independent window groups. Without a partition, the window can operate over all rows. With department partitioning, calculations restart for each department. With patient partitioning, sequence calculations restart for each patient. Partition changes the calculation context, not the number of output rows by itself. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: ORDER BY inside OVER
slides.transcript: ORDER BY inside OVER is part of the analytical definition. For ranking, it defines higher and lower positions. For LAG and LEAD, it defines previous and next. For running totals, it defines the sequence of accumulation. When ordering values can tie, add a stable tie-breaker when deterministic row sequence matters. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: Window frames
slides.transcript: A frame describes which rows within an ordered partition contribute to the current calculation. For a running total, the frame may start at the beginning and end at the current row. For a three-row moving average, it may include two preceding rows and the current row. For some value functions, the frame may need to extend to the end of the partition. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: Ranking functions
slides.transcript: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK look similar until ties occur. ROW_NUMBER always assigns a unique sequence. RANK gives equal values the same rank and leaves gaps afterward. DENSE_RANK also shares ranks but does not leave gaps. Choose the function based on what ties should mean for the business question. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: ROW_NUMBER
slides.transcript: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence even when values tie. This makes it useful for selecting exactly the top two or top three rows per group. But if salaries tie and you only order by salary, the sequence among tied rows may not be deterministic. Add a stable tie-breaker such as employee ID when the order matters. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: RANK
slides.transcript: RANK behaves like a competition ranking. If two employees tie for second, both receive rank two. The next rank is four. This is useful when the numeric rank should reflect positions consumed by the tie. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: DENSE_RANK
slides.transcript: DENSE_RANK also gives tied values the same rank. But it does not leave gaps. If two employees tie for second, the next distinct salary gets rank three. This is often useful for grouping distinct ordered levels. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: Compare ranking ties
slides.transcript: Run this query and focus on rows with the same salary. ROW_NUMBER still gives them different sequence numbers. RANK gives them the same rank and leaves a gap. DENSE_RANK gives the same rank but no gap. This side-by-side comparison makes the business differences visible. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: Deterministic ordering
slides.transcript: Deterministic ordering matters when you use ROW_NUMBER. If two employees have equal salary, salary alone does not define which comes first. Adding employee ID creates a stable order. But be careful with RANK and DENSE_RANK. If you include employee ID inside the ranking ORDER BY, the tied salary rows are no longer peers. Choose the ordering based on the meaning you want. Connect this idea to a sales team calculating running revenue and top products by region. slides.title: Rank within groups
slides.transcript: Partitioning makes ranking local to a group. If we partition by department, each department gets its own rank sequence. An employee can be rank one in Analytics even if someone in Engineering has a higher salary. The comparison set is defined by the partition. slides.title: LAG
slides.transcript: LAG is used when a question contains words such as previous, change, or time since. The current row remains in the result. LAG retrieves a value from an earlier row in the defined order. Partitioning prevents one patient's sequence from mixing with another patient's sequence. The order is part of the definition of previous. LAG and LEAD compare a row with a previous or next row in a defined sequence. The sequence must be meaningful—usually time plus a stable tie-breaker. This is powerful for readmissions, repeat purchases, machine events, and state transitions.

slides.title: LAG admissions example
slides.transcript: This query sequences admissions within each patient. LAG retrieves the previous discharge time. The outer query subtracts that previous discharge from the current admit time. The result is the interval between encounters. The first admission for each patient has no previous discharge, so it is excluded in the final stage. slides.title: LEAD
slides.transcript: LEAD is the forward-looking counterpart to LAG. It retrieves a value from the next ordered row. This is useful for time until next visit, next purchase, or next event. Again, the partition and order define the sequence. LAG and LEAD compare a row with a previous or next row in a defined sequence. slides.title: LEAD visits example
slides.transcript: This query partitions website visits by user and orders them by visit time and visit ID. LEAD retrieves the next visit timestamp. Subtracting the current timestamp gives time to the next visit. The last visit in each user sequence has no next row, so LEAD returns NULL. slides.title: Sequence order must be meaningful
slides.transcript: Sequence analysis depends on order. A timestamp usually defines the main sequence. If two events share the same timestamp, a stable event ID can break the tie. Without a meaningful order, previous and next are undefined from an analytical perspective. Always treat the ordering clause as part of the business logic. slides.title: Running totals
slides.transcript: A running total uses an ordered window frame. The calculation starts at the beginning of the partition and ends at the current row. As the current row moves forward, the frame grows. If we partition by department, each department gets its own running total. Running and moving calculations depend on the window frame. Defaults can be surprising, especially with duplicate ordering values or LAST_VALUE. Write the frame explicitly when the intended range matters. A clear frame makes the query easier to audit and protects against subtle changes in data.

slides.title: Running total SQL
slides.transcript: This query first creates daily revenue by department. Then a window SUM accumulates those daily values. The frame is explicit: from unbounded preceding through the current row. Run it and watch the cumulative revenue increase within each department. The partition restarts the running total for each department. slides.title: Moving averages
slides.transcript: A moving average uses a sliding frame rather than an ever-growing frame. With two preceding rows and the current row, the calculation uses up to three ordered rows. At the beginning of the sequence, fewer than three rows may be available. The frame moves forward with the current row. Running and moving calculations depend on the window frame. Defaults can be surprising, especially with duplicate ordering values or LAST_VALUE. Write the frame explicitly when the intended range matters. A clear frame makes the query easier to audit and protects against subtle changes in data.

slides.title: Moving average SQL
slides.transcript: The daily CTE produces one revenue value per date. The window AVG orders those dates and uses a frame from two preceding rows through the current row. Run the query and compare the raw daily revenue with the smoothed moving average. Remember that this is a three-row window, not necessarily three calendar days if dates are missing. slides.title: ROWS frame
slides.transcript: The ROWS frame counts ordered rows. Two preceding means up to two earlier rows. It does not mean two days, two hours, or two months unless every time unit has exactly one row. This distinction matters when the sequence has gaps. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. slides.title: Explicit frame example
slides.transcript: This query writes the cumulative frame explicitly. It starts at the first row of the ordered partition and ends at the current row. slides.title: LAST_VALUE pitfall
slides.transcript: LAST_VALUE often surprises students. The function does not automatically look to the final row of the partition. It returns the last value in the current frame. With the default ordered frame, that frame commonly ends at the current peer group. If you want the final value across the entire partition, make the frame extend through unbounded following. slides.title: GROUP BY vs PARTITION BY
slides.transcript: GROUP BY and PARTITION BY both organize rows into groups, but they affect output very differently. GROUP BY collapses rows to the grouping grain. PARTITION BY defines a window context while preserving the detail rows. Choose based on the output grain you need, not because window functions are newer or more advanced. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: GROUP BY stay duration
slides.transcript: This query calculates average stay per patient using GROUP BY. The output has one row per patient. Individual admission rows are no longer present. That is correct when the desired output grain is patient level. GROUP BY collapses rows; PARTITION BY does not. That distinction lets you compute group totals, percentages, or rankings while preserving detail. For top-N-per-group problems, rank within each group first and then filter the ranked result in an outer query.

slides.title: PARTITION BY stay duration
slides.transcript: This query keeps each completed admission. It calculates stay days for the admission and also calculates the patient's average stay using a window. The average is repeated beside each admission for that patient. This is useful when you need to compare an individual stay with the patient's usual pattern. Window functions preserve detail rows while calculating across a related set. PARTITION BY defines independent groups, ORDER BY defines sequence, and the frame defines which neighboring rows participate. Those three choices are part of the business rule, not just syntax.

slides.title: Compare output row counts
slides.transcript: This query counts the rows produced by the GROUP BY approach and the window approach. The grouped result has one row per patient. The window result has one row per admission. Neither is automatically better. They answer different analytical output-grain questions. Connect this idea to an operations team comparing each event with the previous and next event. slides.title: Percent of total
slides.transcript: Percent of total is a classic window pattern. Each sale row remains visible. The denominator uses SUM revenue over all rows. Dividing the current row revenue by that total produces the row's contribution percentage. A GROUP BY would not preserve each individual sale row in the same way. GROUP BY collapses rows; PARTITION BY does not. That distinction lets you compute group totals, percentages, or rankings while preserving detail. For top-N-per-group problems, rank within each group first and then filter the ranked result in an outer query.

slides.title: Percent-of-total SQL
slides.transcript: This query calculates each sale's percent of all revenue. SUM revenue OVER empty parentheses means the window covers all returned rows. There is no partition. Each sale remains in the output. Run the query and inspect the largest contributions. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. slides.title: Top N per group
slides.transcript: Top N per group is a common CTE plus window pattern. First calculate a rank inside each group. Then put that ranked result in a CTE. Finally filter the rank in the outer query. The separation is useful because window functions are computed before the outer filtering stage. GROUP BY collapses rows; PARTITION BY does not. That distinction lets you compute group totals, percentages, or rankings while preserving detail. For top-N-per-group problems, rank within each group first and then filter the ranked result in an outer query.

slides.title: Top N with ROW_NUMBER
slides.transcript: This query uses ROW_NUMBER within each department. Salary descending defines the main order. Employee ID breaks exact salary ties deterministically. The outer query filters row number less than or equal to two. That returns at most two rows per department. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Top N including ties
slides.transcript: This version uses RANK instead of ROW_NUMBER. If two employees share the second-highest salary, both can receive rank two and both can pass the rank less than or equal to two condition. That means the output may contain more than two employees in a department. Choose this behavior when ties should be included. Ranking functions differ mainly in how they handle ties. ROW_NUMBER forces a unique sequence, RANK leaves gaps after ties, and DENSE_RANK does not. Add deterministic tie-breakers when a unique order matters; otherwise two executions can choose different rows among tied values.

slides.title: CTE + window pipeline
slides.transcript: CTEs and windows are most useful when combined into a pipeline. The first CTE aggregates revenue to department-product grain. The second stage ranks those product totals inside each department. The final query filters to the top ranks. Each stage has a different job and a clear row meaning. A CTE gives a name to an intermediate result so a complex query can be read in stages. Use it to clarify grain changes and major transformations, not simply to break every two lines into a new block. A useful CTE name describes what the rows represent, such as patient_totals or ranked_visits.

slides.title: Pipeline SQL
slides.transcript: The product totals CTE creates one row per department and product. The ranked CTE keeps the same grain but adds DENSE_RANK within each department. The final SELECT filters to the top two rank groups. Run the query and trace the grain through all three stages. This is a strong example of readable advanced SQL. slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript: Use this checkpoint to connect business questions with SQL patterns. Named stages suggest CTEs. Hierarchies suggest recursion. Group context beside detail suggests window functions. Previous-event questions suggest LAG. Top N per group suggests ranking in one stage and filtering in another. The pattern choice should follow the analytical question. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything. State what one output row should represent, which records you expect to remain, and what edge case is most likely to expose a mistake. Then run the SQL and compare the result with that prediction. slides.title: Grain checkpoint
slides.transcript: The GROUP BY versus PARTITION BY choice is fundamentally a grain decision. If you want one row per patient, GROUP BY may be correct. If you need every admission and the patient average beside it, a window is a better fit. Ask whether detail should be collapsed or preserved. slides.title: Ranking checkpoint
slides.transcript: Ranking functions should be chosen from the tie rule. If you need exactly two rows, ROW_NUMBER is appropriate. If tied second-place employees should all be included, RANK fits better. If you want compact rank levels without gaps, use DENSE_RANK. The business meaning of ties determines the function. slides.title: Sequence checkpoint
slides.transcript: Sequence analysis needs two things before LAG or LEAD can make sense. First, define whose sequence you are analyzing with PARTITION BY. Second, define the event order. Then choose LAG for a previous value or LEAD for a next value. If the order is ambiguous, the sequence result is ambiguous too. For this activity, make a prediction before you run anything. slides.title: Advanced SQL decision guide
slides.transcript: Use this guide when selecting advanced SQL tools. Named stages suggest CTEs. Hierarchies suggest recursive CTEs. Detail plus group context suggests windows. Top N requires a ranking rule. Previous and next suggest LAG and LEAD. Running and moving calculations require ordered windows and meaningful frames. And if you truly want one row per group, GROUP BY may still be the simplest correct choice. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time.
